## Why Your Med Spa Phone Number Is More Valuable Than You Think


Your clinic's phone number appears in more places than you might expect: Google Business Profile, your website footer, patient reminder texts, your Instagram bio, all tied to your[med spa practice management](https://decodahealth.com/who-we-serve/med-spa) setup, and old Groupon listings that still drive calls years later.


That number has built recognition over time. Patients have it saved. When it changes, that recognition disappears with no clean way to notify everyone at once.


> "Changing your business phone number is one of the most disruptive things you can do, because your old number is woven into the fabric of how patients find and contact you."


The good news: when switching practice management software, your number[can move with you](https://www.ccivoice.com/blog/can-i-keep-my-phone-number-with-voip) through a process called porting.


## What Phone Number Porting Actually Is


Porting is the process of moving your existing phone number from your current carrier or software system to a new one, with the digits staying exactly the same. Your patients keep calling the same number. You just answer it somewhere new.


This right is protected by federal law. The Telecommunications Act of 1996 created local number portability, and the FCC requires that carriers[cannot refuse a valid porting request](https://www.phone.com/the-complete-guide-to-porting-your-business-phone-number/) . You own your number. No carrier can hold it hostage because you decided to switch.


For a med spa switching practice management software, this matters a lot. You are not asking permission. You are exercising a right that has existed for decades.


## Porting vs. Call Forwarding: Why the Difference Matters for a Clinic Transition


Call forwarding redirects incoming calls from your old number to a new one, but your old number stays with your old carrier. There is now a relay in the middle, and that relay depends on your old provider staying active and cooperative.


Porting moves the number itself. As[Vonage explains](https://www.vonage.com/resources/articles/how-number-porting-lets-you-keep-your-old-number-for-your-new-services/) , once a port completes, your number lives entirely inside the new system with no dependency on a vendor you are leaving.


Forwarding can work as a bridge during a transition window, but practices that rely on it indefinitely end up maintaining an account with a provider they no longer use, a problem that compounds when front desk capacity is already stretched thin. That old account eventually lapses, gets cancelled, or the forwarding silently breaks. Port the number, and use forwarding only if you need a few days of overlap while the port completes.

## What You Need to Gather Before Starting a Port


Before you submit a porting request, you need a handful of documents ready. Missing any one of them will stall the process.


- The exact business name as it appears on your current phone bill (not your trade name or DBA, unless that is what the bill says)
- Your service location on file with the current carrier
- Your account number
- A recent billing statement
- A signed Letter of Authorization (LOA)


The LOA formally authorizes your new provider to request the number transfer from your old carrier on your behalf. Most new providers supply a template.


The detail that trips people up most often: every field on your LOA must match your current account exactly. A missing comma, an abbreviated "St." versus "Street," or the wrong entity name is enough for a carrier to reject the request outright. Pull up your most recent bill before filling out anything, and copy the fields character by character.


## The Realistic Porting Timeline


FCC rules require simple ports to be processed within one business day, but[business ports take 7 to 14 days](https://www.affiliatedcom.com/blog-keep-business-phone-numbers-switching-providers) in practice. Practices with multiple lines or less common carrier configurations should expect the longer end of that range.


The part that catches practice owners off guard: the timeline is almost entirely controlled by your losing carrier, not your new provider. Submit the porting request in week one if your go-live date is four weeks out, and use the overlap window to configure automated reminders that help[reduce med spa no-shows](https://decodahealth.com/blog/how-to-reduce-med-spa-no-shows) from day one.


## Common Reasons Port Requests Get Delayed or Rejected


Most rejections trace back to one root cause: a mismatch between your LOA and what your losing carrier has on file. "LLC" versus "L.L.C." A street location with a suite number your carrier never recorded. A business name that uses an ampersand on the bill but "and" on your authorization form.


Other frequent causes include a pending account change, an outstanding balance, a number still under an active contract, or an incorrect PIN.


None of these are fatal. A rejection is a correction notice, not a hard stop. Fix the detail, resubmit, and the clock restarts. Pull your current bill before touching the LOA, and read every field as if you are filing a legal document, because functionally, you are.

## What Happens to Fax Numbers During a Platform Migration


Fax numbers run on the same underlying phone infrastructure as voice lines, so they can technically be ported. The catch is that not every practice management system is set up to receive them.


Some systems support inbound fax through a dedicated module or a third-party integration. Others have no fax capability at all, meaning your fax number would have nowhere to land even if a port were initiated. Practices routing lab orders, referrals, or prescriptions through fax need to verify this before signing anything, and understanding[how AI handles inbound faxes](https://decodahealth.com/blog/ai-fax-classification-routing) can shape how you plan that workflow.


Decoda Health does not support fax number porting. Clinics migrating from a system that assigned a fax number will lose that number in the transition, so set up an alternative fax service before your go-live date.


Ask any prospective vendor directly: "Can I port my existing fax number into your system, and does it support inbound and outbound fax natively?" A vague answer is a signal to keep pressing.


## How to Keep Patients Informed Without Missing a Call During the Transition


The porting window is where most practices introduce unnecessary risk, and it almost always comes from the same mistake: canceling the old carrier too early.


Keep your old phone service fully active until you receive written confirmation that the port is complete. "We submitted the paperwork" is not confirmation. Your old number stays live and answerable until your new system confirms the number is live on its end.


A few steps that protect you during the window:


- Use your new system's temporary number for all internal testing and staff training before cutover day
- Brief your front desk on what cutover day looks like, since there is typically a brief window where calls may route inconsistently
- Do not announce a new number to patients; the whole point of porting is that the number never changes
- Set up[missed call text-back](https://decodahealth.com/products/communications) on your temporary number during testing so the workflow is ready the moment your real number ports in


Patients, handled correctly, should never know a transition happened.
